detail:
The University of Birmingham's Birmingham Clinical Trials Unit presents IIH:WT, the IIH Weight Trial, a randomised controlled trial testing whether weight loss is an effective, sustainable treatment for idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). The trial randomised 64 participants 1:1 between two pathways: bariatric surgery, delivered through local NHS bariatric services, and a community weight management programme (Weight Watchers), with vouchers provided for the diet programme arm.

The trial enrolled women with a body mass index above 35 with active, chronic IIH, defined in the source by optic disc swelling (papilloedema) and raised intracranial pressure, who had previously tried other non-surgical approaches to lose weight without maintaining the loss. The primary outcome was the change in intracranial pressure between baseline and 12 months; because of the nature of the interventions the trial was open label, while assessors of visual, cognitive, and sleep apnoea tests were blinded to treatment group. Participants were followed for five years, with visual symptoms and headaches among the outcomes tracked.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about intracranial hypertension research and clinical trials.
summary: The University of Birmingham describes IIH:WT, a randomised trial of 64 women with active IIH comparing bariatric surgery with a community weight management programme, with change in intracranial pressure at 12 months as the primary outcome.
takeaways: the trial randomised participants between surgery and a diet programme
the primary outcome was change in intracranial pressure at 12 months
research participation is optional; talk to your doctor about studies
title: Intracranial Hypertension: the IIH:WT trial of weight loss as treatment
